utterances.text: And those two sets of remains that we see in the water there, are they not broadly in the position where you saw two bodies floating on the 8th of September?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Being under oath, there were bodies in the canal.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I don't really think I can be more specific than that to be honest at this late stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand that, and I don't want to press you for more detail than you feel comfortable giving. But it is quite important that we get as much information as you feel that you can reliably give, because I don't know whether you were aware of this but these two bodies never showed up on any of the forensic reports prepared by the Serbian forensic team. And I wanted to ask you whether the bodies that you saw in the canal when you arrived there, whether there was any serious attempt being made to retrieve them out of the water?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived on the afternoon of this date, there were bodies, as I said in my initial report, between six to 12, some in the water and some on the banks of the canal. How many were actually in the water at this stage --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You don't know.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it's impossible to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, that's a very fair answer. Some were in the water. I think earlier on in your testimony you thought that there were certainly three bodies in the concrete section of the canal in the water and one lower down in the natural area of canal in the water. That was your recollection when you gave evidence in chief, but let us not press you for information that you're not comfortable providing. But can I just ask you this: In your situation report, and obviously you're not a pathologist, you've seen a fair number of dead bodies in your time, Colonel Crosland?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sadly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In your estimate, the bodies you saw, rather like these two bodies, were bodies that were anything up to one month old, could be less, but anything up to one month old. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I have written. I can see your point and where you are coming from; but with the conditions prevailing at the time, the heat, bodies can deteriorate very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. No. I'm not coming from anywhere. I'm simply clarifying with you. Of course, they could be more recent than one month old?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But from what you saw, the bodies you saw looked as if the oldest of them was about a month old?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I've written in the report and that is what, in considering, when I wrote the report, would be as accurate as I could -- as someone familiar with bodies, sadly, but obviously not an expert in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, of course not. But that would take us roughly to the offensive of Gllogjan and Irzniq that you looked at on the BBC film, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could take you back to that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You picked up some ammunition and you identified it as Chinese ammunition, and you made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, before you continue, could you give me the source of the number of bodies. I'm looking at page 2972 at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There I find not exactly what --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: 2972, line 10, and then there's further evidence at 2977.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I might have missed that. Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: 2977, line 8, down to 2978, line 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll read it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You collected a handful of shell-casings which had Chinese writing on them and appeared to you to be Chinese ammunition. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And your initial thought was that that was an indication of KLA involvement in the action at the canal. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was widely thought that part of the ammunition involved by the KLA, and remembering the Balkans is awash with ammunition from all parts of the world, that this could indicate - and I think I did say could indicate --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- KLA activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I think at one point, in one of your witness statements, you also indicated that it wasn't known, at least as far as you were concerned, that the Serb forces were either using Chinese ammunition or issuing Chinese ammunition to their forces. That was not a fact that was known?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not a fact that was known.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No. Just one point of clarification for a moment. You were -- you sent the ammunition casings back to London, and you got a response. Now, you were asked about this in chief, and I think it may be a slip of the tongue in your reply. But at 2973 of the transcript, you were asked about your results and you said: "I think, as far as I recall, it came back that they were Albanian, it was Albanian ammunition, which was no great surprise." Now, did you mean to say Albanian or did you mean to say Chinese?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think both could have --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's not what it says. It says at page -- the answer was:" I think. I can't remember now. It was that the ammunition had come from Albania, which is of no great surprise."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's not the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let's just clarify the position, because it was Chinese round. I just want to be clear. When it came back from the forensics in London, what were you being told that it was Chinese ammunition or were you being given any specific information about where it could be sourced to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, sir, that it was Chinese ammunition that appeared to have come from Albania, bearing in mind that Albania had imploded or exploded in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, that may well be defaulted by other people, but that's as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Have you ever heard - and you talked about propaganda activities by the Serbs in order to engage in dirty tricks to implicate the other side in the conflict, and I asked you some questions about that - have you ever heard of the Serb forces being issued with Chinese rounds in order to attribute crimes to the KLA during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please, behind tab 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This is a document that needs to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number D86, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: As you can see, Colonel Crosland, this is an ambush plan. It is authored by Lieutenant-Colonel Djordjevic, and it relates to an ambush that is planned to take place in January 1999. And if one looks towards the top, one sees the involvement of the department of state security in this operation and that it is to be directed at terrorists located in Jablanica and, amongst other places, Glodjane. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you see under heading, "Method of execution," it's an operation that's going to be executed by the PJP combining or comprising particular ambush positions. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then if we turn to page 3, can you see: "Preparations for execution"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I'll read it into the record: "On the 23rd of January, 1999, the platoon leader and the squad leaders of PJP, together with a sector leader from the Celopek PO, shall make a reconnaissance of the area and the ambush locations. The platoon leader of PJP shall provide grenade launchers and ammunition manufactured in China. While immediately prior to the execution of the task, he shall inspect the forces and acquaint them with the Plan and specific tasks." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: A little further down under, "Equipment, weapons, and MTS: "Members of the PJP shall wear green camouflage uniforms, heavy-duty boots, bullet-proof vests, be equipped with long-barrelled weapons with two BKs." Do you see that, two BKs, that is two combat ammunition sets? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "While each squad should have one hand-held launcher and 30 bullets manufactured in China." Colonel Crosland, can you help us as to any legitimate reason why ambush squads of that kind should be issued both with two combat ammunition sets and with 30 bullets where the country of manufacture is specified as China?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems very odd. The only person who can answer that is Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It seems very odd because specifying Chinese ammunition would be picked up by someone like you as a sign that the KLA was responsible. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could well be used as an indicator, yes, as I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And was used by you, entirely properly, as an indicator at the canal site. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes, as stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Would this fall within that general rubric of dirty tricks that you were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could this fall within that general rubric of dirty tricks that you were referring to in the witness statement where you commented that such things had been done before?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would seem fairly effective evidence to that fact, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. For Your Honour, that is paragraph 19 of the June 2006 statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I have just one or two further questions, if I may, and on other topics. First of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, again, the abbreviation MTS appears, which seemed to be unclear formerly and had not been explained by the interpreters. I would suggest to you to seek verification of the following suggestion that it stands for "materijalno tehnicka sredstva," which would be kind of a general expression for military equipment. I'm not an expert. I didn't hear it from an expert, but it was a suggestion made which perhaps is worthwhile to verify.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm very grateful, and we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want just -- in the few minutes remaining, I just want to ask you one or two other questions. First of all, you gave evidence in chief about the date when you first met Ramush Haradinaj in Gllogjan, and I just want to see if I can explore the date with you, because when first asked about this you said that without reference to a contemporary report of yours, you couldn't remember the date. You may remember that it came up that none of us actually had a contemporary report from you recording that first meeting. It may be one of the documents that hasn't been provided. But in the absence of a note, you were asked by Mr. Re to approximate when it was that the first meeting took place, and your estimate at that point was that you thought it might be about March or April. And I want just to see if I can understand, in the absence of your notes, the degree of approximation that was involved in those dates; in other words, I want to try, if I can with you, to establish what the margin for error is on the dates you gave us. I appreciate that in doing so you can't remember the exact dates, so what I'm looking for a parameters of the approximation. First of all, can we take it for certain that your first meeting with Ramush Haradinaj was before your visit to the canal?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your approximation was March or April. Could it have been May?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may well have been, sir. As I say, life has moved on since then and I'm afraid details like that escape me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's what I need to understand. I'm not putting a particular date to you, but could it have been as late as June or July?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want to look, if I can, at tab 21 in the bundle to see if that helps you. It doesn't tell us when this meeting happened. It might tell us whether or not it had happened by the 17th of June at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that it's to be assigned an exhibit number under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, exhibit number under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number D87, marked for identification and under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's only going to take me -- there's just one passage I wanted to take you to. Tab 21. Do you see paragraph 4, you refer to certain events in Malisevo and then the main road; and then about five lines down, there is a sentence that reads: "The area around Glodjane east of Decani may also be under KLA control, but is not accessible to foreigners." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That was the 17th of June. Do you think it's possible -- I'm sorry. I've given you the -- just check if I've got the right date. 23rd of June, I apologise, that was the 23rd of June. Can I correct the transcript, please. Tab 21 is the 23rd of June. Does that assist? Because if you were saying then that you didn't know whether Gllogjan Glodjane was at that point under KLA control because it was inaccessible to foreigners, I mean, might that be an indication that you hadn't, in fact, met Mr. Haradinaj at that time in Glodjane?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. First of all, this telegram is signed by David Landsman, who is the deputy head of mission and is, I would suggest, a political comment on the KLA control.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I'm afraid I can't agree with your assessment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well, very well. You thought when you gave evidence in chief that at the time of the first meeting, Mr. Haradinaj was what you described as I think commander of the Dukagjin area, and I'm going to put to you: We've seen documents in this case from the KLA side, the authenticity of which are not in dispute, which show Mr. Haradinaj being elected as commander of the Dukagjini Plain on that very day, the 23rd of June. So what I'm trying to explore with you is whether at the time of your first meeting you were in a position to describe his role within any formal organisational structure or simply had an impression of him as a local leader?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only way I can answer that, sir, is that in various statements I have made, I indicated that other intelligence sources were putting together a picture of the possible organisation of the KLA from external sources. Those of us who were working within the province of Kosovo were attempting to add, as everyone does in an intelligence-gathering operation, pieces of information that may or may not have been confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't, in all honesty, be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, well that's what I wanted to establish. How broad were the parameters of uncertainty. I think the intelligence document you're referring to was a British military intelligence OrdBat, which you referred to in the past as a guesstimate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that was produced sometime in the middle of the summer, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so, sir, yes. I'm sorry. I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. Two other short questions before quarter to, if I may. First of all, in the statement you made in March of this year, you said that: "In the early part of 1998, the KLA as a whole was not particularly well-organised. At that stage, the KLA was more locally focused." And I just want to ask you what that expression "locally focused" meant.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think what I was trying to portray was the picture of intelligence that we were putting together in what was a very difficult and demanding situation, and that the areas that then had been engaged by the Serbian security forces; namely, the Drenica and the western parts of Kosovo, drew our attention in particular to those areas. Therefore, one was attempting to put some kind of formation and characters to various positions that they may or may not have held.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that was the next question I was going to ask you, and the final one. In a statement that you made in June 2006, you said this - and I'll just quote the passage - "It seemed like the ranks and hierarchy of the KLA might have been just for show, to create a semblance of organisation and depth to us internationals." Can I ask you, please, shortly just to explain what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on those occasions when we saw more formed bodies of KLA around in Malisevo or wherever, then for propaganda purposes, maybe, they would, as any organisation would do, they would put on a show to show that they were perhaps more organised than inwardly they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We've seen a document from the 23rd of June, for example, and it is only an example, that ascribes to a particular individual, the function of being in charge of atomic, biological, and chemical defence within the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I sincerely hope he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Is that the sort of rank for show you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Being serious, the intelligence organisations need to try and brief their seniors on what the potential threat of that particular organisation may be; and therefore, sensible - and I would respectfully submit to the Court that nuclear, chemical, biological warfare was not a sensible statement - the more sensible approach was to try and ascertain what the capabilities of this organisation was. Therefore, we would look at it and try and piece together the intelligence picture to provide a realistic without over-egging their ability, but at the same time trying to make it clear to the international community that the Serbs were possibly facing a serious problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which, you know, has accrued.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLOND [Resumed]
utterances.text: So one, I think, would hope that our intelligence assessments were both logical and correct and sensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Mr. Re wants to raise something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just a clarification, the transcript on page 3745 actually says: "Appointed head of biological and chemical defence." Mr. Emmerson was reading from a particular document. There was no mention of nuclear or atomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Two translations. I didn't use the word nuclear, atomic, biological, and chemical. There were two translations of that document because there were two sets of minutes for that meeting. I think Mr. Re will find - I may be the one who's in error - but I suggest that I'm not the one who is wrong. So we can check it. May I indicate, Your Honour, that I've run over by five minutes I've got five minutes literally left. I won't propose to do it today but could I trespass on your patience for five minutes in the morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, how much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think quite realistically, and I will be reviewing the transcript, I believe I will be asking, probably, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But if I'm asking any questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that estimate would change, would you please inform us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Informally, because whether or not five more minutes will be granted to Mr. Emmerson, may also depend on what your intentions are, since it has been again and again said to us your estimate for today was a combined estimate of you and Mr. Emmerson. So, therefore, if you would like to put questions to the witness tomorrow, then we'd like to know how much time that would need and we have in the back of our mind that we have to decide on the request of Mr. Emmerson to grant him another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Why don't I do this at this time because I've been going through those areas that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The other Trial Chamber is waiting, Mr. Guy-Smith, and we take it that you have serious reasons to do it as you do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Crosland, we finish for the day. Even in view of what happened over the last two or three minutes, you don't have to be afraid that it would more than a part of tomorrow's session. Travelling back and forth is not something that the Chamber would like you to do. I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony given until now and still to be given tomorrow. We stand adjourned. We'll resume tomorrow, 24th of May, 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
